_comment: The 45-minute recorded talk. Each segment shows its presenterm deck, then drives the agent through one or more turns. Slides never print a result: the numbers arrive live, so the prompts can stay exploratory without the deck contradicting them.

segments.title: What we are about to do
Look at it before you touch it
turns: There are ten CSV files in hospitals/. Do not write a converter and do not fix anything yet. Read enough of them to tell me what you notice, and rank what you find by how much damage it would do if nobody caught it.

segments.title: Three dialects, one table
turns: Now build the single table. You decide the schema and tell me what you chose. Two things I care about: how you decide which file is which dialect, and what you do with the fields that only some sites record.
How many patients ended up in each arm, and did you lose anyone along the way?

segments.title: The obvious comparison
turns: Compare overall survival between the two arms the simplest way you can. No adjustment at all. Give me the hazard ratio and tell me in one sentence what a reader would conclude from it.
Do you believe that number? Show me whatever would convince you either way.

segments.title: Making the arms comparable
turns: The two arms are not the same kind of patient. Handle it. Tell me your plan before you run anything, then run it and report how many patients you had to leave behind.
You sorted the treated patients before matching. Which direction did you sort, and does it matter? Try the other one.
So which of those two numbers is the right one to publish?

segments.title: Why a curve and not a percentage
turns: Give me the survival difference in the matched cohort, and give it to me in whatever form you think a clinician should see. Save any figure you make.
What fraction of each arm was still alive at twelve months, and how does that compare with just counting who died? Explain the gap.

segments.title: Subgroups test consistency
turns: Break the result down by the subgroups a reviewer would ask about. Do not go hunting: decide the list first and tell me it, then run them.
Is there a subgroup that benefits more than the others? Answer carefully.

segments.title: Try to break your own result
turns: Someone will say you picked the analysis that worked. Hold the data completely fixed, vary every analytic choice you can defend, and show me the whole distribution rather than your favourite point.
Which of those runs would you throw away, and why? Give me the honest summary after you have thrown them away.

segments.title: Writing it down, from the log
turns: Write the Methods section. Reconstruct it from the scripts you actually ran, not from what you meant to do, and mark anything you cannot source.
Now the Results. Every number has to come from a file on disk, and I want to see which file each one came from.

segments.title: Let it review its own work
turns: Open four reviewers in parallel, in one message: statistical, clinical, reporting standards, reproducibility. They may read the manuscript and the output files here and nothing else. Ask each for a recommendation and its three strongest objections, one line each.
Of everything they raised, which findings are real defects in the work rather than matters of taste? Fix one of them now.
